title: Leftmost-Fit Memory Blocks
statement:
Simulate a tiny memory of n units, numbered 0 to n − 1. At the start every unit is free.

  • Allocator(n) creates the memory.
  • allocate(size, owner) finds the leftmost run of size consecutive free units, gives them to owner and returns the index of the first unit. If no such run exists, nothing changes and it returns -1.
  • release(owner) frees every unit that owner holds, across all of its blocks, and returns how many units were freed (0 if it held none).

One owner may hold several separate blocks. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the allocator. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: After owner 2 frees units 3–4, there are 3 free units in total (3, 4 and 7) but no 3 in a row, so size 3 fails. Size 2 fits at 3. Owner 1 then frees both of its blocks: 3 + 2 = 5 units.
Releasing an owner that holds nothing frees 0 units. A request bigger than the whole memory fails.

hints: The memory is small. What is the most direct way to represent which owner holds each unit?
Keep an array where cell i holds the owner of unit i, or 0 if free. To allocate, scan left to right, counting the current run of free units.
When the run reaches size, the block starts at i − size + 1. To release, clear every cell that holds the owner and count them.

explain.intuition:
With at most 1000 units and 1000 calls, the plain simulation is the intended answer: one array, mem[i] = owner or 0 for free. An allocation is a single left-to-right scan that counts how many free units it has seen in a row; the moment that count reaches size, the leftmost fitting block ends here. Freeing is a scan that clears an owner's cells.

When memory gets big, keep a sorted list of free intervals instead (like a real allocator's free list), and a map from owner to its blocks. Then allocate walks free intervals, not units, and release gives back whole blocks, merging neighbours so free space does not stay fragmented.
steps: allocate(size, owner): keep run = 0. For each i, set run = mem[i] === 0 ? run + 1 : 0. When run === size, fill mem[i − size + 1 .. i] with owner and return i − size + 1.
release(owner): set every mem[i] === owner to 0, count them, and return the count.
pitfalls: Checking total free space instead of consecutive free space. The first example has 3 free units but no run of 3.
Releasing only the owner's most recent block. release frees every block the owner holds.
Not resetting the run counter when a used unit is met.

solutions.title: Array of owners
solutions.idea: mem[i] holds the owner of unit i or 0. Allocate by scanning for a free run; release by clearing the owner's cells.

solutions.title: Free list of intervals
solutions.idea: Keep free space as sorted [start, end) intervals and a map from owner to its blocks. Allocate from the first interval that is long enough; on release, add the blocks back and merge touching intervals.
solutions.time: O(f) per allocate, O(f log f) per release, f = free intervals

followups: Memory has 10⁹ units and calls are 10⁵. Which structure finds the leftmost long-enough free interval in O(log n)? (Hint: a segment tree storing the longest free run.)
Allocate into the smallest free interval that fits (best fit) instead of the leftmost. What changes?
